claim: A polymorphism in APP that reduces APP processing protects from sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD) and normal aging-dependent decline.
source: In humans, a polymorphism in APP that reduces APP processing protects from sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD) and normal aging-dependent decline (Supplementary file 1; Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jonsson et al., 2012, which is referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in APP and in genes that regulate APP processing are causative of AD pathology.
source: In contrast, mutations in APP and in genes that regulate APP processing are causative of AD pathology (van der Kant and Goldstein, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van der Kant and Goldstein, 2015.

claim: APP is a transmembrane protein that undergoes extracellular cleavage by one of two activities, α- or β-secretase.
source: APP is a transmembrane protein that undergoes extracellular cleavage by one of two activities, α- or β-secretase, resulting in the formation of large N-terminal extracellular fragments of secreted APP and smaller, membrane-bound C-terminal fragments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about APP processing.

claim: The membrane-retained C-terminal fragments are subjected to an intramembranous scission by the γ-secretase complex to generate the APP intracellular domain (AICD).
source: Subsequently, the membrane-retained C-terminal fragments are subjected to an intramembranous scission by the γ-secretase complex (Wolfe et al., 1999) to generate the APP intracellular domain (AICD) and simultaneously release p3 (after α-secretase cleavage) or amyloid-β peptide (Aβ, after β-secretase cleavage).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wolfe et al., 1999.

claim: A new secretase activity, called η-secretase, cleaves APP primarily at amino acids 504–505 of APP695.
source: In collaboration with other teams, we also recently described a new secretase activity, called η-secretase (Willem et al., 2015). Cleavage by η–secretase occurs primarily at amino acids 504–505 of APP695 and releases a ~ 500 amino acid-long ectodomain and a membrane-bound fragment called CTF-η, which is further processed by α- and β- secretases to release a long and a short Aη peptide (Aη-α and Aη-β, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Willem et al., 2015.

claim: APP processing is regulated by synaptic activity.
source: Importantly, APP processing is regulated by synaptic activity (Kamenetz et al., 2003; Cirrito et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamenetz et al., 2003 and Cirrito et al., 2005.

claim: One of the early neurochemical changes in AD is the dysfunction of cholinergic and glutamatergic synapses, which correlates with cognitive decline ante mortem.
source: and one of the early neurochemical changes in AD is the dysfunction of cholinergic and glutamatergic synapses, which correlates with cognitive decline ante mortem (Selkoe, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Selkoe, 2002.

claim: APLP1 and APLP2 display strong similarity to APP within the cytoplasmic domain.
source: When studying APP function, a confounding factor is the presence of the functionally redundant APP-like protein-1 and -2 (APLP1 and APLP2), which display strong similarity to APP within the cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about APP family proteins.

claim: APLP1 and APLP2 are processed like APP and release intracellular peptides that can potentially regulate gene transcription.
source: APLP1 and APLP2 are processed like APP (Müller and Zheng, 2012) and release intracellular peptides that, like AICD, can potentially regulate gene transcription (Scheinfeld et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Müller and Zheng, 2012 and Scheinfeld et al., 2002.

claim: Mice lacking the last 15 amino acids of APP (APP-CT15 domain) in an APLP2-KO background (APPΔCT15-DMs) present hippocampal synaptic deficits.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the APP intracellular domain might play a crucial role on synapse physiology, given that mice lacking the last 15 amino acids of APP (APP-CT15 domain) in an APLP2-KO background (APPΔCT15-DMs) present hippocampal synaptic deficits.
evidence: The claim is based on previously published research.

claim: APPΔCT15-DMs mice showed impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), apparently due to post-synaptic alterations, and deficits in spatial working memory.
source: In particular, these mice showed impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), apparently due to post-synaptic alterations, and deficits in spatial working memory (Klevanski et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klevanski et al., 2015.

claim: AICD is very short (~50 amino acids), but includes important sequence motifs and adapter protein-binding sites.
source: AICD is very short (~50 amino acids), but includes important sequence motifs and adapter protein-binding sites (Grimm et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grimm et al., 2015.

claim: AICD is unstable and difficult to isolate and characterize biochemically.
source: This 6 kDa peptide is unstable, hence difficult to isolate and characterize biochemically (Belyaev et al., 2010; Flammang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Belyaev et al., 2010 and Flammang et al., 2012.

claim: Cleavage of APP in endosomes, through BACE1-dependent amyloidogenic processing, generates an AICD fragment capable of inducing nuclear signaling.
source: However, studies on cells, in vitro, demonstrated that cleavage of APP in endosomes, through BACE1-dependent amyloidogenic processing, generates an AICD fragment capable of inducing nuclear signaling (Goodger et al., 2009; Grimm et al., 2015; Kimberly et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goodger et al., 2009, Grimm et al., 2015, and Kimberly et al., 2001.

claim: AICD shuttles to the nucleus via binding of the highly conserved YENPTY motif to the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65.
source: In line with these findings, AICD was shown to shuttle to the nucleus, via binding of the highly conserved YENPTY motif to the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65, but whether AICD harbors transcriptional activity remains controversial (Cao and Südhof, 2001, Cao and Südhof, 2004; Riese et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao and Südhof, 2001, Cao and Südhof, 2004, and Riese et al., 2013.

claim: AICD plays a critical physiological role in controlling GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors (NMDARs) at immature excitatory synapses, via a transcription-dependent mechanism.
source: We report a critical physiological role of AICD in controlling GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors (NMDARs) at immature excitatory synapses, via a transcription-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: AICD increase in mature neurons, as reported in AD, alters synaptic NMDAR composition to an immature-like GluN2B-rich profile.
source: We further show that AICD increase in mature neurons, as reported in AD, alters synaptic NMDAR composition to an immature-like GluN2B-rich profile.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AICD-induced alteration of synaptic NMDAR composition disrupts synaptic signal integration, via over-activation of SK channels.
source: This disrupts synaptic signal integration, via over-activation of SK channels, and synapse plasticity, phenotypes rescued by GluN2B antagonism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AICD-induced synaptic phenotypes are rescued by GluN2B antagonism.
source: This disrupts synaptic signal integration, via over-activation of SK channels, and synapse plasticity, phenotypes rescued by GluN2B antagonism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GFP mRNA expression was similar in GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons.
source: On average, GFP mRNA expression was similar in GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 1C; left side of panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by single cell quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increased expression of mRNA representing the C-terminal domain of APP was observed in AICD and AICD-NLS neurons.
source: As expected, increased expression of mRNA representing the C-terminal domain of APP was observed in AICD and AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 1C; right side of panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by single cell quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio was significantly decreased in AICD neurons.
source: This ratio was significantly decreased in AICD neurons, an effect that was more pronounced in AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decrease in AMPAR/NMDAR ratio was more pronounced in AICD-NLS neurons compared to AICD neurons.
source: This ratio was significantly decreased in AICD neurons, an effect that was more pronounced in AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neurons transduced with AICD-NES presented an AMPAR/NMDAR ratio similar to GFP neurons.
source: Neurons transduced with AICD-NES presented an AMPAR/NMDAR ratio similar to GFP neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 682 in the 682YENPTY motif within AICD was necessary for the synaptic phenotype.
source: Phosphorylation of tyrosine 682 in the 682YENPTY motif within AICD, which regulates binding of cytoplasmic proteins such as Fe65 (Grimm et al., 2013), was necessary for this synaptic phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Grimm et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons expressing AICDY682G exhibited a normal AMPAR/NMDAR ratio.
source: Indeed, we created an AAV expressing AICD with an Y682G mutation (same AAV vector as in Figure 1A) and neurons expressing AICDY682G exhibited a normal AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: APLP2-ICD, but not APLP1-ICD, lowered the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio.
source: Interestingly, APLP2-ICD, but not APLP1-ICD, lowered the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AICD affects excitatory post-synaptic transmission via its nuclear activity and phosphorylation of its tyrosine 682.
source: Together, these data show that AICD, via its nuclear activity and phosphorylation of its tyrosine 682, affects excitatory post-synaptic transmission, a function also displayed by the APLP2 C-terminal domain, but not that of APLP1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: AICD does not affect AMPAR transmission.
source: One could observe similar amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs, suggesting that AICD does not affect AMPAR transmission (Figure 2B–D, Supplementary file 1, one way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by miniature EPSC analysis shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: AICD-NLS neurons exhibited unchanged AMPAR EPSCs.
source: AICD-NLS neurons exhibited unchanged AMPAR EPSCs, confirming the results obtained with AMPAR mEPSC analysis (Figure 2F and G; Supplementary file 1; matched-pairs Student's t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by pairwise comparison data shown in Figures 2F and G.

claim: NMDAR EPSCs were markedly increased in AICD-NLS neurons.
source: whereas NMDAR EPSCs were markedly increased (Figure 2H and I; Supplementary file 1, matched-pairs Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by pairwise comparison data shown in Figures 2H and I.

claim: Enhanced AICD production in CA1 pyramidal neurons increases NMDAR synaptic transmission, while AMPAR function is not affected.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that enhanced AICD production in CA1 pyramidal neurons increases NMDAR synaptic transmission, while AMPAR function is not affected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: AICD-NLS neurons exhibited a slower deactivation time course than GFP neurons.
source: AICD-NLS neurons exhibited a slower deactivation time course than GFP neurons (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by NMDAR EPSC deactivation kinetics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AICD-NLS neurons showed a significant increase in τslow and τweighted without noticeable changes in τfast.
source: an effect mediated by a significant increase in τslow and τweighted (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA), without noticeable changes in τfast (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMDAR EPSC deactivation kinetics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AICD causes alterations in NMDAR transmission due to an increase of synaptic GluN2B currents.
source: These results suggest that AICD causes alterations in NMDAR transmission due to an increase of synaptic GluN2B currents.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the deactivation kinetics data.

claim: Ifenprodil (5 µM) significantly reduced NMDAR EPSC amplitude in AICD-NLS neurons, being much less effective in GFP neurons.
source: Ifenprodil (5 µM) significantly reduced NMDAR EPSC amplitude in AICD-NLS neurons, being much less effective in GFP neurons (Figure 3B,E; Supplementary file 1; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figures 3B and E.

claim: Application of ifenprodil normalized the deactivation kinetics in AICD-NLS neurons while not significantly perturbing NMDAR kinetics in GFP neurons.
source: Moreover, application of ifenprodil, while not significantly perturbing NMDAR kinetics in GFP neurons, normalized the deactivation kinetics in AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 3A,B; Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: Enhanced AICD production leads to a specific increase in synaptic NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits.
source: Enhanced AICD production thus leads to a specific increase in synaptic NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ifenprodil experiments.

claim: There is a dose-dependent relationship between acute application of TAT-AICD-NLS and levels of synaptic GluN2B currents with IC50 ~13.88 ± 1.65 nM.
source: We observed a dose-dependent relationship between acute application of TAT-AICD-NLS and levels of synaptic GluN2B currents (i.e. effect of ifenprodil on NMDAR EPSC) with IC50 ~13.88 ± 1.65 nM (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Doses as low as 30 nM TAT-AICD-NLS were sufficient to reach maximal incorporation of GluN2B within synapses (~50% of NMDAR current).
source: Notably, doses as low as 30 nM were sufficient to reach maximal incorporation of GluN2B within synapses (~50% of NMDAR current) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Pre-incubation with TAT-AICD-NES (100 nM) did not significantly increase the contribution of GluN2B-NMDAR to the NMDAR EPSC.
source: Importantly, pre-incubation with TAT-AICD-NES (100 nM) did not significantly increase the contribution of GluN2B-NMDAR to the NMDAR EPSC (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The effect of AICD on synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR is dependent on AICD presence in the nucleus.
source: suggesting that this effect is dependent on AICD presence in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TAT-AICD-NES experiment.

claim: TAT-AICD-NLS failed to increase synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR currents in the presence of actinomycin or anisomycin.
source: As shown in Figure 3E (Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA), TAT-AICD-NLS failed to increase synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR currents in the presence of these inhibitors
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The effect of AICD on synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR is transcription and translation-dependent.
source: confirming that the effect of AICD on synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR is transcription and translation-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the actinomycin and anisomycin experiments.

claim: TAT-AICD-NLS is enriched in the nucleus compared to TAT-AICD-NES.
source: As expected (Figure 3H,I, Supplementary file 1, Student's t-test), TAT-AICD-NLS was enriched in the nucleus compared to TAT-AICD-NES.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figures 3H and I.

claim: AICD regulates the transcription of Grin2b, the gene encoding the GluN2B subunit.
source: Our data strongly suggest that AICD could regulate the transcription of Grin2b, the gene encoding the GluN2B subunit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: SynAICD-expressing hippocampi displayed a significant increase in endogenous GluN2B mRNA levels compared to synGFP-expressing hippocampi.
source: Importantly, SynAICD-expressing hippocampi displayed a significant increase in endogenous GluN2B mRNA levels compared to synGFP-expressing hippocampi (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1, Student's t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AICD over-expression correlates with increased Grin2b expression.
source: correlating AICD over-expression to increased Grin2b expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the qPCR data.

claim: Ifenprodil was devoid of effect in cells expressing shAPP-active, indicating that loss of APP induces a complete absence of synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs.
source: In contrast, ifenprodil was devoid of effect in cells expressing shAPP-active, indicating that loss of APP induces a complete absence of synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs (Figure 5E,H; Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 5E and H.

claim: Neurons expressing shAPP-active exhibited a faster deactivation time course than neurons expressing shAPP-inactive.
source: Confirming this, neurons expressing shAPP-active exhibited a faster deactivation time course than neurons expressing shAPP-inactive (Figure 5F)
evidence: The claim is supported by NMDAR EPSC deactivation kinetics data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TAT-AICD-NLS fully normalized GluN2B levels at synapses in neurons expressing shAPP active.
source: Notably, TAT-AICD-NLS fully normalized GluN2B levels at synapses as ifenprodil significantly decreased the amplitude of NMDAR EPSCs (~50%) in neurons expressing shAPP active (Figure 5G,H; Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5G and H.

claim: Ex vivo delivery of nuclear AICD is sufficient to restore the physiological profile of GluN2B-NMDARs at immature synapses in the absence of APP.
source: Thus, ex vivo delivery of nuclear AICD is sufficient to restore the physiological profile of GluN2B-NMDARs at immature synapses in the absence of APP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TAT-AICD-NLS rescue experiment in shAPP-active neurons.

claim: Pre-incubation with TAT-AICD-NLS does not further enhance synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs levels in neurons expressing the control inactive shAPP.
source: As shown (Figure 5H; Supplementary file 1, one-way ANOVA), pre-incubation with TAT-AICD-NLS does not further enhance synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs levels in these neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: APP acts via AICD to govern synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs levels.
source: suggesting that APP acts via AICD to govern synaptic GluN2B-NMDARs levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The amount of TAT-AICD-NLS incorporated in hippocampal slices after 2 hr incubation was ~10 pg per µg of tissue lysate.
source: As shown (Figure 6C), the amount of TAT-AICD-NLS incorporated in hippocampal slices after 2 hr incubation was ~10 pg per µg of tissue lysate
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The amount of TAT-AICD-NLS incorporated in hippocampal slices is approximately twofold the concentration obtained for adult (5 months old WT) brain tissue lysate, representing adult physiological levels.
source: which is approximately twofold the concentration we obtained for adult (5 months old WT) brain tissue lysate, representing adult physiological levels (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: An increase of AICD in mature neurons has been reported in human AD brains and AD mouse models.
source: An increase of AICD in mature neurons has been reported in human AD brains and AD mouse models (Ghosal et al., 2009; Lauritzen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ghosal et al., 2009 and Lauritzen et al., 2012.

claim: There is an approximately fivefold increase of AICD in Tg2576 brains at 5 months old, when comparing to the adult physiological controls.
source: We could clearly observe an approximately fivefold increase of AICD in Tg2576 brains, when comparing to the adult physiological controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The addition of TAT-AICD-NLS to endogenous AICD levels in mature neurons could reach an AICD concentration in the range of values observed in the Tg2576 AD mouse model.
source: Importantly, this quantitative analysis demonstrates that the addition of TAT-AICD-NLS to endogenous AICD levels in mature neurons (adult physiological AICD levels + TAT-AICD-NLS levels) could reach an AICD concentration in the range of values observed in the Tg2576 AD mouse model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AICD quantification data.

claim: GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons exhibited similar mean EPSP amplitudes at low frequencies (0.1 and 1 Hz).
source: GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons exhibited similar mean EPSP amplitudes at low frequencies (0.1 and 1 Hz) (Figure 7A and B, Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 7A and B.

claim: At 10 Hz, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons exhibited a decrease in mean EPSP amplitude after the second pulse compared to GFP neurons.
source: At 10 Hz, however, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons exhibited a decrease in mean EPSP amplitude after the second pulse compared to GFP neurons (Figure 7C, Supplementary file 1, two-way ANOVA multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: AICD and AICD-NLS neurons presented a significant decrease in AP discharge probability upon stimulation at 50 Hz.
source: Moreover, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons presented a significant decrease in AP discharge probability upon stimulation at 50 Hz (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In dendritic spines, NMDARs form an intimate Ca2+-mediated feedback loop with SK2.
source: In dendritic spines, NMDARs form an intimate Ca2+-mediated feedback loop with SK2 (Köhler et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Köhler et al., 1996.

claim: Synaptic SK2 channels and NMDARs colocalize within 25–50 nm in the post-synaptic densities of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Synaptic SK2 channels and NMDARs colocalize within 25–50 nm in the post-synaptic densities of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SK2-NMDAR coupling.

claim: SK2-NMDAR coupling allows for a tight negative regulation of NMDAR effects in spines, favoring rapid Mg2+ reblocking of NMDARs, thus limiting the amplitude of synaptic potentials and reducing Ca2+ transients, especially for stimulation frequencies higher than 5 Hz.
source: This SK2-NMDAR coupling allows for a tight negative regulation of NMDAR effects in spines, favoring rapid Mg2+ reblocking of NMDARs, thus limiting the amplitude of synaptic potentials and reducing Ca2+ transients, especially for stimulation frequencies higher than 5 Hz (Figure 8A) (Stackman et al., 2002; Mateos-Aparicio et al., 2014; Hammond et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stackman et al., 2002, Mateos-Aparicio et al., 2014, and Hammond et al., 2006.

claim: Apamin (100 nM) increased the mean amplitude of EPSPs in GFP neurons.
source: As illustrated in Figure 8B and C, apamin (100 nM) increased the mean amplitude of EPSPs in GFP neurons, as previously reported by others at this synapse (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Hammond et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 8B and C, and citations to Ngo-Anh et al., 2005 and Hammond et al., 2006.

claim: Apamin-induced potentiation of neurons was significantly stronger in AICD-NLS than in GFP neurons.
source: Apamin-induced potentiation of neurons was significantly stronger in AICD-NLS than in GFP neurons (Figure 8B and C; Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 8B and C.

claim: Blocking GluN2B with ifenprodil (5 µM) completely abolished the apamin effect in AICD-NLS neurons.
source: Moreover, blocking GluN2B with ifenprodil (5 µM) completely abolished this effect (Figure 8B and C; Supplementary file 1; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 8B and C.

claim: There is over-activation of synaptic SK channels in AICD neurons due to excessive presence of GluN2B-NMDARs.
source: We thus evidenced over-activation of synaptic SK channels in AICD neurons due to excessive presence of GluN2B-NMDARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the apamin and ifenprodil experiments.

claim: Signal integration and discharge probability phenotypes at 10 Hz and above were rescued by partial blockade of GluN2B-NMDARs with ifenprodil (300 nM) or blockade of SK channels with apamin (100 nM).
source: As illustrated (Figure 8D–G; Supplementary file 1, two-way ANOVA and multiple comparisons), these phenotypes were rescued by partial blockade of GluN2B-NMDARs with ifenprodil (300 nM) or blockade of SK channels with apamin (100 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 8D-G.

claim: Increasing AICD production alters synaptic signal integration and AP discharge probability at 10 Hz frequencies and above, impairment due to excessive GluN2B-NMDARs and SK channel functions.
source: Together, these results show that increasing AICD production alters synaptic signal integration and AP discharge probability at 10 Hz frequencies and above, impairment due to excessive GluN2B-NMDARs and SK channel functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD), induced by low-frequency stimulation (1 Hz), was equivalent in GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons.
source: As expected, long-term depression (LTD), induced by low-frequency stimulation (1 Hz), was equivalent in GFP, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons (Figure 9A,B, Supplementary file 1; one-way ANOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 9A and B.

claim: AICD and AICD-NLS neurons could not maintain LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation (100 Hz).
source: By contrast, AICD and AICD-NLS neurons could not maintain LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation (100 Hz; Figure 9C,D, Supplementary file 1; one-way ANOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 9C and D.

claim: 300 nM ifenprodil fully rescued LTP in AICD-NLS neurons.
source: By contrast, a bell-shape effect was observed in AICD-NLS neurons and 300 nM ifenprodil fully rescued LTP (Figure 9E,F, Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1 ; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 9E, F and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: AICD-dependent synaptic alterations spare LTD but strongly perturb LTP, a phenotype that is normalized by partial GluN2B antagonism.
source: Therefore, AICD-dependent synaptic alterations spare LTD but strongly perturb LTP, a phenotype that is normalized by partial GluN2B antagonism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LTD and LTP experiments.

claim: AICD exerts its effect at synapses via a nuclear-dependent mechanism.
source: We, therefore, conclude that AICD exerts its effect at synapses via a nuclear-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of AICD, AICD-NLS, and AICD-NES effects.

claim: AICD is stabilized by the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65, which enables AICD to translocate to the nucleus.
source: Accordingly, there is evidence that AICD is stabilized by the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65, which enables AICD to translocate to the nucleus (Kimberly et al., 2001; Cupers et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimberly et al., 2001 and Cupers et al., 2001.

claim: APP and APLP2 more readily co-localize than APLP1 with APP in intracellular compartments such as endosomes.
source: Of note, APLP2 more readily co-localizes than APLP1 with APP in intracellular compartments such as endosomes (Kaden et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaden et al., 2009.

claim: APP and APLP2, but not APLP1, harbor a phosphorylation-dependent Pin1-binding site, which is implicated in APP C-terminal conformation and in Fe65 binding.
source: Also, APP and APLP2, but not APLP1, harbor a phosphorylation-dependent Pin1-binding site, which is implicated in APP C-terminal conformation and in Fe65 binding (van der Kant and Goldstein, 2015; Pastorino et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van der Kant and Goldstein, 2015 and Pastorino et al., 2006.

claim: Knocking down APP during a particular developmental window does not permit compensation by other APP family members.
source: In accordance with our data, these authors could show that knocking down APP during a particular developmental window does not permit compensation by other APP family members, thus uncovering APP physiological roles that are otherwise masked by compensation in germline APP KOs.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Callahan et al., 2017.

claim: APP expression levels peak in the second post-natal week.
source: Also, the developmental role of APP in mammalian development persists after birth, as APP expression levels peak in the second post-natal week (Löffler and Huber, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Löffler and Huber, 1992.

claim: APP expression levels peaking in the second post-natal week coincides with the timing of the NMDAR developmental switch.
source: Strikingly, it coincides with the timing of the NMDAR developmental switch (Williams et al., 1993), suggesting that APP might play a role in this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 1993.

claim: Addition of the β-secretase-derived βAPP fragment (C99), precursor of Aβ and AICD, decreased NMDAR currents.
source: This finding is in apparent disagreement with the observation reported by Hoe et al. (2009) where addition of the β-secretase-derived βAPP fragment (C99), precursor of Aβ and AICD (Wolfe et al., 1999), decreased NMDAR currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoe et al., 2009 and Wolfe et al., 1999.

claim: Aβ was shown to decrease synaptic NMDARs in cultured neurons.
source: These opposite effects may be due to concomitant generation of Aβ, which was shown to decrease synaptic NMDARs in cultured neurons (Snyder et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Snyder et al., 2005.

claim: The APP intracellular domain associated-1 protein (AIDA-1) is implicated in endoplasmic reticulum export of GluN2B-containing NMDARs to synapses.
source: Also, it was shown that the APP intracellular domain associated-1 protein (AIDA-1) is implicated in endoplasmic reticulum export of GluN2B-containing NMDARs to synapses (Tindi et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tindi et al., 2015.

claim: Over-expression of APP resulted in enhanced cell surface NMDAR expression, which was not GluN2-subunit specific.
source: and that over-expression of APP resulted in enhanced cell surface NMDAR expression, which was not GluN2-subunit specific (Cousins et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cousins et al., 2009.

claim: Over-expression of APLP1 and APLP2 resulted in enhanced cell surface NMDAR expression.
source: an effect that was also observed with over-expression of APLP1 and APLP2 (Cousins et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cousins et al., 2015.

claim: APP over-expression and alterations in APP processing are linked to synaptic dysfunction and/or cognitive deficits in trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) in humans.
source: Several human studies have linked APP over-expression and alterations in APP processing to synaptic dysfunction and/or cognitive deficits. This is observed in trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) in humans (McCarron et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McCarron et al., 2014.

claim: APP over-expression and alterations in APP processing are linked to synaptic dysfunction and/or cognitive deficits in trisomy 16 in mice.
source: and trisomy 16 in mice (Cataldo et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cataldo et al., 2003.

claim: Duplication of the APP locus is observed in rare familial autosomal dominant AD cases and de novo genetic variations.
source: It is also true for rare familial autosomal dominant AD cases (Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2006) and de novo genetic variations (Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2015), where duplication of the APP locus has occurred.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2006 and Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2015.

claim: Autosomal dominant genetic mutations observed in familial AD cases point to increased processing of APP via the amyloidogenic pathway.
source: Also, autosomal dominant genetic mutations observed in familial AD cases (e.g. KM670/671 NL Swedish mutation, A673V mutation; E682K Leuven mutation) and susceptibility loci discovered through genome-wide association studies (e.g. ATXN1) point to increased processing of APP via the amyloidogenic pathway (Citron et al., 1992; Di Fede et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011; Bertram et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Citron et al., 1992, Di Fede et al., 2009, Zhou et al., 2011, and Bertram et al., 2010.

claim: AICD and other APP fragments accumulate in brains from individuals with Trisomy 21.
source: Accordingly, besides Aβ, AICD and other APP fragments accumulate in brains from individuals with Trisomy 21 (Sun et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2006.

claim: AICD and other APP fragments accumulate in brains of humans diagnosed with AD.
source: in brains of humans diagnosed with AD (Willem et al., 2015; Ghosal et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Willem et al., 2015 and Ghosal et al., 2009.

claim: AICD and other APP fragments accumulate in APP over-expressing AD mouse models.
source: and in APP over-expressing AD mouse models (Willem et al., 2015; Lauritzen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Willem et al., 2015 and Lauritzen et al., 2012.

claim: AICD is difficult to detect biochemically and unstable.
source: However, it is well known that AICD is difficult to detect biochemically and unstable (Hébert et al., 2006; Giliberto et al., 2010; Waldron et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hébert et al., 2006, Giliberto et al., 2010, and Waldron et al., 2008.

claim: AICD could participate in excessive NMDAR function observed in APP over-expressing and presenilin mutant mouse models of AD.
source: Notably, AICD could participate in excessive NMDAR function observed in APP over-expressing and presenilin mutant mouse models of AD (Marchetti and Marie, 2011; Kaczorowski et al., 2011; Lanté et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marchetti and Marie, 2011, Kaczorowski et al., 2011, and Lanté et al., 2015.

claim: An AICD-dependant mechanism could be the target of the NMDAR-GluN2B antagonist memantine.
source: An AICD-dependant mechanism could also be the target of the NMDAR-GluN2B antagonist memantine (Xia et al., 2010) commonly used for more than a decade to prevent declines in cognition, behavior and autonomy in AD patients, albeit with modest efficacy (Matsunaga et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xia et al., 2010 and Matsunaga et al., 2015.

claim: Low nanomolar concentrations of AICD in mature neurons are sufficient to disrupt synapse signaling.
source: Moreover, we show that low nanomolar concentrations of AICD in mature neurons are sufficient to disrupt synapse signaling, thus raising the likelihood that AICD contributes to the AD synaptic failure, together with other APP fragments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
